document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 34-year-old man is assessed at a walk-in clinic. When asked why he came in today, he gives long replies about his neighbours, the weather, and a television program. Each reply drifts away from the question and he never returns to the original point, although his sentences remain grammatically intact and he denies racing thoughts. Which term best describes this abnormality of thought form?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines tangential speech as speech that is oblique or irrelevant and does not come back to the original point, in contrast to circumstantial speech, which is indirect and delayed in reaching its goal but eventually returns to the point. This man's replies wander from the question and never return, which is tangentiality.

optionExplanations.a: Circumstantial speech is indirect and delayed but does eventually come back to the point, which is not the case here.
optionExplanations.c: Flight of ideas is quick skipping from one marginally connected idea to another, usually with racing thoughts in mania, which he denies.
optionExplanations.d: Perseveration is repetition of the same verbal or motor response to stimuli, not drifting away from the topic.
optionExplanations.e: Thought blocking is a sudden cessation of the flow of thought and speech, which is not described.

source.reference: PS4 — Mental Status Exam: Thought Process/Form

questions.question: A 46-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after telling a friend he would be better off dead. He smells strongly of alcohol, is dysarthric and unsteady on his feet, and says he no longer wants to be alive but will not answer questions about a plan or about access to means. Vital signs and physical examination are otherwise unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step in his risk assessment?

options.text: Base the risk formulation on the account he gives while intoxicated
Reassess his suicidal ideation once he is sober
Discharge him now with a crisis line number and outpatient follow-up
Defer any risk assessment until he can be seen in an outpatient psychiatry clinic
Obtain a urine drug screen and discharge him once the result is available

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states explicitly that when assessing risk, if the patient is intoxicated on the first approach, the clinician should reassess when the patient is sober. Assessment of plan, intent, access to means, and protective factors cannot be reliably completed while he is intoxicated, so the assessment is repeated once he is sober and a level of risk and safety plan are then determined.

optionExplanations.a: The source specifically warns that the assessment performed while the patient is intoxicated should be repeated when sober.
optionExplanations.c: Discharge before a reliable risk assessment has been completed does not follow the recommended approach.
optionExplanations.d: Suicide risk must be screened and assessed at the encounter; deferring the whole assessment to an outpatient clinic leaves the risk unassessed.
optionExplanations.e: A drug screen does not substitute for reassessing ideation, plan, intent, and protective factors when sober.

source.reference: PS5 — Suicide: Approach and Assessment of Risk

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman is assessed for a severe major depressive episode. She has lost 9 kg, is profoundly psychomotor retarded, and holds a fixed belief that her internal organs have rotted away and that she deserves to die. She describes active thoughts of ending her life and has been declining fluids for two days. She lives alone. What is the most appropriate management of her risk?

options.text: Outpatient treatment with pharmacotherapy and good supports
Brief crisis intervention in the emergency department followed by discharge
Referral to community group psychotherapy with weekly review
Telephone follow-up by a crisis team the next day

questions.explanation: For patients with depression, Toronto Notes advises considering hospitalization if symptoms are severe or if psychotic features are present; otherwise outpatient treatment with good supports and pharmacotherapy is appropriate. This woman has both severe symptoms and mood-congruent nihilistic delusions with active suicidal ideation, so admission is the appropriate management of risk.

optionExplanations.b: Outpatient management with supports and pharmacotherapy is reserved for depression that is not severe and not psychotic.
optionExplanations.c: Crisis intervention with possible discharge is described for patients with personality disorders, not for severe depression with psychotic features.
optionExplanations.d: Group psychotherapy does not address the immediate safety concern in severe psychotic depression.
optionExplanations.e: Telephone follow-up does not provide the level of supervision indicated when symptoms are severe and psychotic features are present.

source.reference: PS7 — Suicide: Safety Planning and Management by Diagnosis

questions.question: A 21-year-old university student is brought by his parents. Over the past nine months he has withdrawn from friends, stopped attending classes, and expressed increasingly odd beliefs. For the last two months he has stated that a government agency is monitoring him and his speech is frequently derailed. He has never had a depressive or manic episode. Urine drug screen and bloodwork are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DSM-5 criteria reproduced in Toronto Notes require two or more Criterion A symptoms (at least one being delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech) present for a significant portion of a 1 mo period, marked decline in functioning, and continuous signs of the disturbance for at least 6 mo. He has nine months of continuous disturbance with two months of delusions and disorganized speech and functional decline, with mood episodes and substances excluded.

optionExplanations.a: Brief psychotic disorder lasts less than 1 mo with eventual full return to premorbid functioning.
optionExplanations.b: Schizophreniform disorder applies when the episode lasts more than 1 mo but less than 6 mo; his disturbance has been continuous for nine months.
optionExplanations.d: Schizoaffective disorder requires a major mood episode concurrent with Criterion A, and he has never had a depressive or manic episode.
optionExplanations.e: Delusional disorder involves one or more delusions without the other Criterion A features such as disorganized speech and marked functional decline.

source.reference: PS8 — DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria for Schizophrenia

questions.question: A 27-year-old man with schizophrenia has had three relapses requiring hospital admission in two years. Each relapse followed his stopping oral risperidone within weeks of discharge. When he takes the medication his positive symptoms remit fully and he tolerates it well. He has never failed an adequate trial of an antipsychotic taken as prescribed. What is the most appropriate next step in his pharmacological management?

options.text: Switch to a long-acting injectable antipsychotic
Add lithium to the oral risperidone
Add a long-term benzodiazepine to the oral regimen

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that long-acting injectable (depot) antipsychotics have been shown to be more effective in reducing relapse and rehospitalization compared with oral alternatives. This man's relapses are driven by non-adherence rather than by lack of efficacy, so converting to a long-acting injectable directly targets the cause of his relapses.

optionExplanations.b: Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance, and he responds well to risperidone when he actually takes it.
optionExplanations.c: Mood stabilizers such as lithium are listed as adjuncts for aggression or impulsiveness, not for non-adherence.
optionExplanations.d: Anxiolytics are adjunctive agents and do not address relapse driven by stopping the antipsychotic.
optionExplanations.e: ECT is an adjunctive option in resistant or life-threatening presentations, not the first response to non-adherence.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man is admitted after ten days of abnormally elevated and expansive mood with markedly increased goal-directed activity. He has been sleeping three hours a night and feels rested, speaks rapidly and cannot be interrupted, states he has been chosen to lead a global business, and has spent his savings on equipment. He had a major depressive episode at age 24. Urine drug screen is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with mixed features

questions.explanation: A manic episode requires a distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity or energy lasting at least 1 wk (or any duration if hospitalization is necessary), plus at least 3 Criterion B symptoms and marked impairment. He meets these criteria over ten days, and Toronto Notes notes that at least one lifetime manic episode is required for a diagnosis of bipolar I disorder.

optionExplanations.b: Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode and no manic episodes; his episode caused marked impairment and required hospitalization.
optionExplanations.c: Cyclothymia involves numerous hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet full episode criteria.
optionExplanations.d: Mixed features describe concurrent depressive and manic symptoms within an episode and would not exclude the manic episode he clearly meets.
optionExplanations.e: Schizoaffective disorder requires delusions or hallucinations in the absence of a major mood episode, which is not described.

source.reference: PS11 — DSM-5 Criteria for Manic Episode

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with six weeks of depressed mood, anhedonia, insomnia, fatigue, poor concentration, and guilt. Her symptoms are of moderate severity and are interfering with her work. She has no history of a manic or hypomanic episode, no psychotic features, and no suicidal ideation. Bloodwork including TSH is normal. She agrees to start medication. What is the most appropriate initial medication?
questions.explanation: For major depressive disorder of moderate or greater severity, Toronto Notes lists most second generation antidepressants as first line, with escitalopram, mirtazapine, sertraline, venlafaxine, agomelatine, and citalopram showing evidence for superiority. Escitalopram is therefore an appropriate first choice for this uncomplicated moderate episode.

optionExplanations.b: Tricyclic antidepressants are not among the first line second generation agents listed for moderate MDD.
optionExplanations.c: MAOIs are reserved for moderate to severe depression that does not respond to other antidepressants.
optionExplanations.d: Aripiprazole is listed as an augmenting agent for non-response or partial response, not as initial monotherapy.
optionExplanations.e: Lithium is used for bipolar disorder and as augmentation of antidepressants, not as initial treatment of MDD.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman is seen six weeks after an uncomplicated delivery. Her mood began to drop about ten days postpartum and for the past four weeks she has had persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, guilt, and complete disinterest in her infant. She has no hallucinations or delusions and no thoughts of harming the baby. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major depressive disorder with peripartum onset

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that the peripartum onset specifier applies to a major depressive episode with onset during pregnancy or within 4 wk following delivery, and that severe symptoms may include complete disinterest in the baby. Her episode began ten days postpartum and has persisted for four weeks with full depressive features, so this is major depressive disorder with peripartum onset.

optionExplanations.a: Postpartum blues begins 2-4 d postpartum, usually lasts about 48 h and up to 10 d, and feelings of inadequacy and anhedonia are usually mild or absent.
optionExplanations.c: Adjustment disorder requires that the disturbance not meet criteria for another mental disorder, and she meets criteria for a major depressive episode.
optionExplanations.d: Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode, which is not described.
optionExplanations.e: Her presentation is dominated by depressed mood, anhedonia, and guilt rather than excessive worry.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman with a documented diagnosis of bipolar II disorder presents with a six-week depressive episode. She has had two previous hypomanic episodes and several depressive episodes, and has never had a manic episode or psychotic symptoms. She is currently taking no psychotropic medication and agrees to start pharmacotherapy. What is the most appropriate initial medication?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists lithium, lurasidone, quetiapine, and lamotrigine as agents for treating bipolar depression and notes specifically that quetiapine is first line in treating bipolar II depression. It also states that monotherapy with antidepressants should be avoided in bipolar disorder because patients can switch from depression into mania.

optionExplanations.b: Antidepressants are second line in bipolar depression and should only be used with a mood stabilizer, never as monotherapy.
optionExplanations.c: The same caution applies to venlafaxine; antidepressant monotherapy risks a switch into mania.
optionExplanations.d: Haloperidol is not listed among the agents used to treat bipolar depression.
optionExplanations.e: Benzodiazepines are listed for acute agitation in mania, not for treating a bipolar depressive episode.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman describes recurrent unexpected episodes of palpitations, sweating, trembling, chest discomfort, shortness of breath, and a fear of dying. The episodes come on abruptly, peak within minutes, and settle after about ten minutes. For the past three months she has worried persistently about having further episodes and has stopped exercising in case one is triggered. Cardiac and thyroid investigations are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DSM-5 criteria in Toronto Notes define panic disorder as recurrent unexpected panic attacks, an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort reaching a peak within minutes with four or more characteristic symptoms, with at least one attack followed by 1 mo or more of persistent concern about additional attacks or a significant maladaptive change in behaviour related to the attacks. She meets both criteria.

optionExplanations.b: Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by pervasive worry rather than discrete unexpected surges peaking within minutes.
optionExplanations.c: Agoraphobia requires marked fear or anxiety about two or more of the five specified situations such as public transportation, open spaces, or crowds.
optionExplanations.d: Specific phobia involves fear cued by a particular object or situation, whereas her attacks are unexpected.
optionExplanations.e: Illness anxiety disorder involves preoccupation with having a serious disease despite negative investigations, not recurrent panic attacks.

source.reference: PS16 — DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria for Panic Disorder

questions.question: A 40-year-old man with schizophrenia requires a change of antipsychotic because of persistent positive symptoms on his current agent. He has type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 34 kg/m2, and he developed marked drug-induced parkinsonism on a previous antipsychotic. He has never had an adequate trial fail because of lack of efficacy. Which antipsychotic is the most appropriate choice?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes aripiprazole as having less weight gain and risk of metabolic syndrome compared to olanzapine and a lower incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms compared to haloperidol. Given this man's diabetes, obesity, and previous extrapyramidal symptoms, aripiprazole best avoids both the metabolic and the extrapyramidal risks.

optionExplanations.b: Olanzapine causes weight gain and metabolic effects and the source advises avoiding it in diabetes.
optionExplanations.c: Risperidone carries the highest risk of extrapyramidal symptoms and tardive dyskinesia among the second generation agents and should be avoided in patients at high risk of EPS.
optionExplanations.d: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness, causes the most weight gain, and requires ongoing blood count monitoring because of agranulocytosis.
optionExplanations.e: Haloperidol is a high potency typical antipsychotic with a higher incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms.

source.reference: PS51 — Table 15: Commonly Used Atypical Antipsychotics

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman describes intrusive, unwanted thoughts that her hands are contaminated. She recognizes the thoughts as her own and as excessive, but relieves the anxiety by washing her hands in a fixed sequence, now occupying more than two hours each day and making her late for work. Her hands are chapped and cracked. She has no depressive or psychotic symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial psychological treatment?

options.text: Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention

questions.explanation: Her obsessions and compulsions take more than 1 h/d and cause impairment, meeting the DSM-5 criteria for obsessive-compulsive disorder set out in Toronto Notes. The listed psychological treatment for OCD is CBT using exposure and response prevention, in which the patient is exposed to feared situations while the compulsive behaviours are prevented, combined with cognitive strategies that challenge underlying beliefs.

optionExplanations.b: Supportive therapy uses empathy and validation to aid coping and is indicated for adjustment, somatic symptom, and severe psychotic or personality disorders.
optionExplanations.c: Interpersonal therapy focuses on how interpersonal relationships affect symptoms and is indicated for mood disorders.
optionExplanations.d: Dialectical behavioural therapy is the therapy indicated for borderline personality disorder and severe emotional dysregulation.
optionExplanations.e: Psychodynamic therapy explores the meaning of early experiences and is not the specific first line therapy for OCD.

source.reference: PS19 — Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: Criteria and Treatment

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman is assessed four months after a motor vehicle collision in which she was seriously injured. She reports recurrent intrusive memories of the crash, distressing dreams about it, and flashbacks. She avoids driving and avoids conversations about the accident, feels persistently detached from her family, and is hypervigilant with an exaggerated startle response and disturbed sleep. She has stopped working. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: She has exposure to a traumatic event with intrusion symptoms, persistent avoidance, negative alterations in cognitions and mood, and marked alterations in arousal and reactivity, causing significant impairment. Toronto Notes states that the duration of criteria B, C, D, and E must be more than 1 mo, and her symptoms have persisted for four months.

optionExplanations.b: Acute stress disorder describes symptoms persisting from 3 d to 1 mo after exposure to a trauma; she is four months out.
optionExplanations.c: Adjustment disorder does not apply when the disturbance meets criteria for another mental disorder such as PTSD.
optionExplanations.d: Her symptoms are cued by trauma reminders rather than being recurrent unexpected panic attacks.
optionExplanations.e: Generalized anxiety disorder involves pervasive worry, not intrusive re-experiencing of a specific traumatic event.

source.reference: PS21 — DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

questions.question: A 78-year-old man is reviewed on the ward two days after emergency hip fracture surgery. Over the past 24 hours he has been drowsy and inattentive during the day, unable to sustain a conversation, and disoriented to time and place. At night he is agitated, pulls at his intravenous line, and describes seeing small animals in the room. His daughter says his memory was normal before admission. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease

questions.explanation: DSM-5 criteria in Toronto Notes define delirium as a disturbance in attention and awareness developing over hours to a few days, representing a change from baseline and fluctuating in severity over the day, with an additional cognitive disturbance and evidence of a medical cause. Recent surgery is a listed risk factor, and visual hallucinations are described as organic until proven otherwise.

optionExplanations.b: Dementia has a gradual or stepwise onset over months to years with a normal level of consciousness and attention not affected initially.
optionExplanations.c: Brief psychotic disorder does not feature the fluctuating inattention and clouded consciousness seen here, and a medical cause must be excluded.
optionExplanations.d: Cognitive impairment associated with depression has a subacute onset with normal level of consciousness and intact orientation.
optionExplanations.e: Factors favouring delirium over psychosis include visual hallucinations, acute onset, no previous history of psychosis, and sleep-wake changes, all present here.

source.reference: PS23 — DSM-5 Diagnostic Criteria for Delirium

questions.question: A 72-year-old man is brought by his daughter because of memory problems that began about two months ago. He complains at length about his poor memory. He is alert and fully oriented, wakes at 4 am each morning, has lost interest in his hobbies, and appears psychomotor slowed with a pervasively depressed affect. Cognitive testing shows slowed, effortful responses with recent memory difficulty. There is no fluctuation over the day. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Major neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer's disease
Major neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes Table 3 distinguishes cognitive impairment associated with depression by its subacute onset, normal level of consciousness, intact orientation, difficulty concentrating rather than true inattention, recent memory loss that the patient is more likely to complain about, early morning awakening, and pervasive depressed mood. This man's presentation matches that column.

optionExplanations.b: Delirium has acute onset over hours to days with fluctuating level of consciousness and impaired orientation.
optionExplanations.c: Dementia has gradual or stepwise decline over months to years, typically with low insight rather than prominent complaints of memory loss.
optionExplanations.d: Lewy body disease features early changes in executive function and attention with well-formed visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition, none of which are present.
optionExplanations.e: There is no fluctuation, no clouding of consciousness, and no preceding cognitive decline to suggest a superimposed delirium.

source.reference: PS26 — Table 3: Comparison of Dementia, Delirium, and Cognitive Impairment Associated with Depression

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with known alcohol use disorder and biopsy-proven cirrhosis presents 14 hours after his last drink with tremor, diaphoresis, agitation, nausea, and anxiety. He is afebrile with a heart rate of 108 bpm. His CIWA-A score is in the moderate range. He has no history of withdrawal seizures and no hallucinations. Thiamine has been given. Which medication is the most appropriate for managing his withdrawal?
questions.explanation: The CIWA-A treatment protocol in Toronto Notes uses diazepam as the basic protocol, but specifies that if the patient is over 65 years of age or has severe liver disease, severe asthma, or respiratory failure, a short acting benzodiazepine should be used, with lorazepam 1-4 mg PO/SL/IM q1-2 h. This man is 68 with cirrhosis, so lorazepam is the appropriate agent.

optionExplanations.b: Diazepam is the basic protocol agent but is long acting and is specifically not the choice in patients over 65 or with severe liver disease.
optionExplanations.c: Chlordiazepoxide is also a long-acting benzodiazepine and shares the same limitation in this patient.
optionExplanations.d: Haloperidol is added when hallucinations are present and lowers the seizure threshold; antipsychotics are not useful in alcohol withdrawal delirium.
optionExplanations.e: Clonidine is described for symptomatic management of autonomic features of opioid withdrawal, not for alcohol withdrawal.

source.reference: PS29 — Table 5: CIWA-A Scale Treatment Protocol for Alcohol Withdrawal

questions.question: A 31-year-old man with a five-year history of opioid use disorder has completed three medically supervised detoxifications and relapsed within weeks each time. He is currently using non-prescribed opioids daily and injects intermittently. He is medically stable, is engaged with an addiction counsellor, and asks about long-term treatment. What is the most appropriate long-term pharmacological management?

options.text: A short tapering course of oral morphine with no further pharmacotherapy

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes states that long-term treatment of opioid use disorder may include maintenance treatment with methadone, an opioid agonist, or buprenorphine, a mixed agonist-antagonist, and that the Suboxone formulation combines buprenorphine with naloxone to deter injection. Repeated relapse after detoxification is exactly the situation in which maintenance therapy is indicated.

optionExplanations.b: Clonidine is an alpha-adrenergic agonist used for symptomatic management of the autonomic features of withdrawal, not for maintenance.
optionExplanations.c: A further taper repeats the detoxification approach that has already failed and leaves him with loss of tolerance and overdose risk on relapse.
optionExplanations.d: Naloxone is used for life-threatening CNS and respiratory depression in overdose and would precipitate withdrawal if given regularly.
optionExplanations.e: Benzodiazepines are not a listed treatment for opioid use disorder and add sedative risk.

source.reference: PS30 — Opioids: Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder

questions.question: A 42-year-old man has attended his family physician repeatedly over the past year convinced that he has a brain tumour. His only symptom is an occasional mild headache. Imaging and bloodwork have been normal and he has been reassured several times, yet the conviction returns within days. He checks himself daily and researches symptoms for hours. When asked, he concedes he might be wrong. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes illness anxiety disorder as preoccupation with the fear of having or the idea that one has a serious disease, with convictions persisting despite negative investigations and reassurance, somatic symptoms mild or absent, maladaptive behaviour such as excessive physical checking, and duration greater than 6 mo. Crucially, unlike a delusion, the person can acknowledge the possibility that the feared disease is not present.

optionExplanations.b: Somatic symptom disorder requires one or more distressing somatic symptoms that disrupt daily life; here somatic symptoms are mild.
optionExplanations.c: Conversion disorder involves symptoms or deficits affecting voluntary motor or sensory function that are incompatible with recognized neurological disease.
optionExplanations.d: A delusion is a fixed belief, whereas he is able to acknowledge that the feared disease may not be present.
optionExplanations.e: Factitious disorder involves the intentional production or feigning of signs or symptoms; his symptoms are not consciously produced.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa is seen in clinic. She has restricted her intake further over the past month and continues to fear weight gain. On examination she is cold and thin, blood pressure is 84/56 mmHg lying with a symptomatic postural drop, and her heart rate is 36 bpm. Serum potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and magnesium is low. She denies suicidal ideation. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start an SSRI and review in four weeks
Referral to an outpatient eating disorder day programme
Family-based treatment with monthly weight checks

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists criteria to admit to a medical ward for anorexia nervosa, including hypovolemia requiring intravenous fluid, heart rate below 40 bpm, abnormal serum chemistry such as low potassium or magnesium, and active suicidality. She meets several of these, so medical admission with cautious refeeding and close monitoring for refeeding syndrome is required.

optionExplanations.b: Outpatient CBT is appropriate for medically stable patients and does not address bradycardia and electrolyte derangement.
optionExplanations.c: Medications are of little value in anorexia nervosa itself and would not address the acute medical instability.
optionExplanations.d: A day programme does not provide the medical monitoring needed for a heart rate below 40 bpm and hypokalemia.
optionExplanations.e: Family-based treatment is used primarily in the pediatric system and is not sufficient for a medically unstable patient.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman has a pattern dating to late adolescence of intense, unstable relationships in which she alternately idealizes and devalues people, frantic efforts to avoid being abandoned, chronic feelings of emptiness, mood shifts lasting hours, inappropriate anger, impulsive spending and unsafe sexual behaviour, recurrent self-harm, and transient paranoid ideation when stressed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes borderline personality disorder as a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects with marked impulsivity, requiring five or more features including impulsivity, mood instability, paranoia or dissociation under stress, unstable self-image, labile intense relationships with idealization and devaluation, self-harm, inappropriate anger, frantic efforts to avoid abandonment, and feelings of emptiness. She meets nearly all of these.

optionExplanations.b: Histrionic personality disorder centres on attention-seeking, theatrical, excessively emotional behaviour and shallow rapidly shifting emotions.
optionExplanations.c: Narcissistic personality disorder features grandiosity, need for admiration, entitlement, and lack of empathy.
optionExplanations.d: Antisocial personality disorder requires evidence of conduct disorder before age 15 and a pervasive disregard for and violation of others' rights.
optionExplanations.e: Dependent personality disorder involves an excessive need to be taken care of with clinging, submissive behaviour and difficulty making everyday decisions.

source.reference: PS43 — Table 10: Cluster B Personality Disorders

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy is referred after being suspended from school. Over the past year he has initiated several physical fights, bullied younger students, broken into a neighbour's shed and stolen tools, and deliberately set fire to a fence. He was frequently truant from school before age 13 and has stayed out overnight without permission on several occasions, including in the last month. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Adjustment disorder with disturbance of conduct

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes defines conduct disorder as a pattern of behaviour that violates the rights of others and age-appropriate social norms, with three or more criteria in the past 12 mo and at least one in the past 6 mo, spanning aggression to people and animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious violation of rules. He meets criteria in all four categories with recent rule violation.

optionExplanations.b: Oppositional defiant disorder is a pattern of angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behaviour, and vindictiveness without violation of the basic rights of others.
optionExplanations.c: ADHD is a differential consideration but does not itself account for arson, burglary, and assault.
optionExplanations.d: Antisocial personality disorder requires the patient to be at least 18 years old.
optionExplanations.e: Adjustment disorder requires an identifiable stressor within 3 mo and symptoms that do not meet criteria for another mental disorder.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man is brought to his family physician's office in Ontario by his brother. He has an apparent mental disorder, is responding to unseen stimuli, and told his brother yesterday that he intends to seriously harm himself. He arrived in a t-shirt in freezing weather. He refuses assessment at hospital and wants to leave. The physician has examined him today. Which form is the most appropriate to complete?
questions.explanation: Under the Ontario Mental Health Act as summarized in Toronto Notes, Form 1 is an application by a physician to bring a patient to a schedule 1 facility for psychiatric assessment against the patient's will. It is completed when patients are thought to be in imminent danger of harming themselves or others, or are incapable of self-care, and are suffering from an apparent mental disorder, based on the physician's own observations and facts communicated by others.

optionExplanations.b: Form 2 is an order by a Justice of the Peace to bring a patient to hospital for examination, used when a physician has not examined the patient.
optionExplanations.c: Form 3 is the certificate of involuntary admission, signed by a physician other than the one who completed the Form 1, before the Form 1 expires.
optionExplanations.d: Form 4 is the certificate of renewal of involuntary admission, completed before a Form 3 expires.
optionExplanations.e: Form 5 changes a patient's status to informal or voluntary when the criteria for involuntary admission are no longer met.

questions.topic: Involuntary Admission and Canadian Legal Issues

source.reference: PS60 — Table 22: Common Forms Under the Mental Health Act (in Ontario)

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman who has taken paroxetine 20 mg daily for eight months stopped it abruptly three days ago because she felt well. She now describes dizziness, headache, chills, myalgia, nausea, irritability, mood lability, and insomnia. She is afebrile, her physical examination is unremarkable, and she denies low mood or suicidal ideation. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Restart paroxetine at the dose she was taking and then taper slowly over several weeks
Leave paroxetine stopped and treat the symptoms with an antiemetic and simple analgesia
Prescribe lorazepam for two weeks to cover the symptoms
Restart paroxetine at double the previous dose and stop it again in one week
Switch her immediately to venlafaxine extended-release at an equivalent dose

questions.explanation: Discontinuation syndrome is caused by abrupt cessation of antidepressants and is most common with paroxetine, fluvoxamine, and venlafaxine, the drugs with the shortest half-lives. Symptoms begin within 1-3 days and include anxiety, insomnia, irritability, mood lability, nausea and vomiting, dizziness, headache, tremor, chills, fatigue, and myalgia. Symptoms can be relieved within 24 hours by restarting the antidepressant at the same dosage the patient was taking initially and then initiating a slower taper over several weeks.

optionExplanations.b: Untreated, discontinuation symptoms may last 1-3 weeks, whereas restarting the drug relieves them within 24 hours and allows a controlled taper.
optionExplanations.c: A benzodiazepine does not address the cause; the source directs restarting the antidepressant and tapering more slowly.
optionExplanations.d: Doubling the dose is not what the source recommends, and stopping again after one week would simply reproduce an abrupt cessation.
optionExplanations.e: Venlafaxine is one of the agents most often implicated in discontinuation syndrome because of its short half-life, so switching to it does not solve the problem.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has taken lithium 900 mg daily for four years with previously stable serum levels. Two weeks ago she began taking naproxen regularly for back pain. She now reports a worsening tremor, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, headache, and marked lethargy. She is afebrile and her neurological examination shows no focal deficit. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Serum lithium level drawn 12 hours after her last dose
Complete blood count with differential and platelets

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes lists NSAIDs, thiazides, ACEI, OCP, and metronidazole as agents that decrease lithium clearance and create a risk for lithium toxicity. Her new naproxen plus gastrointestinal upset, tremor, headache, and lethargy, all recognised lithium adverse effects, point to a rising level. Lithium serum levels are monitored and the dose adjusted accordingly, and the sample is always drawn 12 hours after the dose.

optionExplanations.b: Thyroid function and creatinine are monitored every 6 months on lithium, but thyroid testing will not explain an acute change after starting an NSAID.
optionExplanations.c: There is no focal deficit or head injury described, and imaging would not identify the drug interaction responsible.
optionExplanations.d: An EEG is not part of the monitoring the source describes for lithium and would not measure the level.
optionExplanations.e: Baseline CBC with differential and platelets is obtained before starting a mood stabilizer, and blood counts are the monitoring priority for carbamazepine rather than for suspected lithium toxicity.

questions.question: A 33-year-old woman at 26 weeks gestation is admitted with a depressive episode with psychotic features. She has refused food and fluids for five days and is clinically dehydrated. Two adequate antidepressant trials during previous episodes produced no response, and her obstetrician is concerned about medication safety and the need for a rapid response. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: A trial of a third antidepressant at maximum dose

questions.explanation: ECT is described as the fastest and most effective acute treatment of depression, and it is the induction of a generalized seizure using an electrical pulse through scalp electrodes while the patient is under general anesthesia with a muscle relaxant. Its indications include treatment-resistant depression with psychotic features and situations where medications may be unsafe or a rapid response is needed, such as cachexia, severe dehydration, high suicide risk, and pregnancy. There are no absolute contraindications.

optionExplanations.b: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation does not match the efficacy of ECT and would not deliver the rapid response this dehydrated, psychotically depressed patient needs.
optionExplanations.c: Psychotherapy alone is inadequate for a depressive episode with psychotic features and refusal of food and fluids.
optionExplanations.d: She has already failed two adequate antidepressant trials, and a further medication trial neither acts rapidly nor addresses the concern about medication safety.
optionExplanations.e: Deep brain stimulation is listed among experimental treatments for depression, not as an acute treatment for this presentation.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman reports four months of low mood, tearfulness, and poor sleep that began after she separated from her husband, moved cities for a new job, and lost her mother. She has ongoing conflict with her adult daughter and feels she no longer has a role in her family. She has good insight, no psychotic symptoms, and no substance use. Which psychotherapy is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Interpersonal therapy is indicated for mood disorders and focuses on how interpersonal relationships impact symptoms, addressing four key problem areas: grief and loss, role transitions, conflict, and interpersonal deficits. The ideal candidates are individuals with depression or bipolar disorder who have some insight and difficult social functioning, which describes this woman, whose episode is framed by bereavement, role transitions, and conflict. It is delivered as weekly sessions over 12-20 sessions.

optionExplanations.b: Dialectical behavioural therapy is indicated for borderline personality disorder and severe problems of emotional dysregulation, impulsivity, or self-harm, none of which are described.
optionExplanations.c: Motivational enhancement therapy is indicated for substance use disorders and maladaptive behaviour patterns, and she has no substance use.
optionExplanations.d: Psychoanalytic therapy suits patients who are psychologically minded and wish to understand themselves rather than just relieve symptoms, and it is time intensive over several years.
optionExplanations.e: Supportive therapy is aimed at individuals in crisis or with severe symptoms, such as adjustment disorders or severe psychotic or personality disorders, rather than this focal interpersonal presentation.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man is brought in by his wife because for the past year he has shouted and thrashed during sleep. Twice a week he punches and kicks, bruising her and injuring his own hand on the bedside table. When she wakes him he is immediately oriented and alert and describes a vivid dream of being attacked. He snores little and is not sleepy during the day. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder
Non-rapid eye movement sleep arousal disorder with sleep terrors

questions.explanation: Rapid eye movement sleep behaviour disorder is described as arousal during sleep associated with vocalization and/or complex motor behaviours that can cause violent injuries, with rapid orientation and alertness on awakening. His enacted, injurious dream behaviour with immediate alertness fits this pattern. Management includes melatonin, clonazepam, and discontinuation of causative medications such as TCAs, SSRIs, and SNRIs.

optionExplanations.b: Sleep terrors involve incomplete awakening with a panicky scream, relative unresponsiveness to comfort, and amnesia for the episode, whereas he is rapidly oriented and recalls the dream.
optionExplanations.c: Nightmare disorder produces well-remembered dysphoric dreams with rapid orientation on awakening, but not the complex motor behaviours and injuries described.
optionExplanations.d: Obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea causes nonrestorative sleep and excessive daytime sleepiness with snoring and morning headaches, which he does not have.
optionExplanations.e: Restless legs syndrome is an uncomfortable, frequent urge to move the legs at night that is relieved by movement, not dream enactment.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman has had six hospital admissions in two years for unexplained hypoglycemia. Extensive investigations have been unrevealing, and a nurse finds an insulin syringe hidden in her bag. She has no disability claim, no pending litigation, no legal charges, and no work she is avoiding, but she becomes animated and content when the ward team gathers at her bedside. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Factitious disorder is the intentional production or feigning of physical or psychological signs or symptoms; unlike malingering, these patients are not motivated by secondary gain but rather may seek sympathy, nurturance, and attention. Her covert insulin administration is an intentional, voluntary production of illness with no external incentive, and she is gratified by the attention of the care team.

optionExplanations.b: Malingering is the intentional production of false or grossly exaggerated symptoms motivated by secondary gain such as avoiding work, financial compensation, or obtaining drugs, and no external reward is present here.
optionExplanations.c: In somatic symptom and related disorders the symptoms are produced unconsciously and are not the result of malingering or factitious disorder, which are disorders of voluntary presentation.
optionExplanations.d: Illness anxiety centres on preoccupation with having a disease rather than deliberately inducing signs of one.
optionExplanations.e: Conversion symptoms are also produced unconsciously and lack objective medical support, whereas she is deliberately injecting insulin.

source.reference: PS33 — Somatic Symptom and Related Disorders

questions.question: A 63-year-old woman is seen after her landlord reported that her apartment is unsafe. For many years she has been unable to discard newspapers, empty containers, and clothing regardless of their actual value, saving them because discarding creates intense distress. Possessions now clutter her kitchen and bedroom so that these active living areas cannot be used. She has no intrusive contamination thoughts and no washing or checking rituals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hoarding disorder is persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of actual value, with a felt need to save items and distress created by discarding, resulting in possessions cluttering and compromising active living areas and causing clinically significant distress or functional impairment. The diagnosis requires ruling out brain injury, cerebrovascular disease, OCD, MDD with low energy, psychotic disorder with delusions, and neurocognitive disorder. Her accumulation is driven by the need to save rather than by obsessions or rituals, and her active living areas are compromised, so hoarding disorder fits.

optionExplanations.b: OCD is an explicit rule-out; her saving is not driven by intrusive obsessions and there are no washing or checking compulsions.
optionExplanations.c: MDD is a rule-out in which clutter accumulates from low energy, not from a need to save items and distress on discarding.
optionExplanations.d: Neurocognitive disorder is a rule-out; there is no cognitive decline here, and the clutter reflects deliberate saving of possessions.
optionExplanations.e: Body dysmorphic disorder is preoccupation with perceived flaws in physical appearance with repetitive behaviours such as mirror checking or excessive grooming.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman is seen seven weeks after the death of her husband. She is tearful, sleeps poorly, and says she misses him constantly. Twice she has transiently heard his voice calling her name and once briefly saw his image in the hallway. She feels sad but denies worthlessness, has no psychomotor retardation, and continues to run her home and see friends. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Support and watchful waiting, with education and normalization of the grief process
Start an antidepressant for her depressed mood
Prescribe an anti-anxiety medication for her distress and insomnia
Start an antipsychotic to treat the hallucinatory experiences
Refer for treatment of persistent complex bereavement disorder

questions.explanation: In bereavement, support and watchful waiting should be first line, along with education and normalization of the grief process; normal grief should not be treated with antidepressant or anti-anxiety medications because it is important to allow the person to experience the whole mourning process to achieve resolution. Hearing the voice or transiently seeing the image of the deceased is within normal bereavement, whereas abnormal grief or MDD is suggested by morbid preoccupation with worthlessness, marked psychomotor retardation, or prolonged and marked functional impairment, none of which she has. Management should still include assessment for secondary conditions such as PTSD, depression, suicidal ideation, and increased substance use.

optionExplanations.b: Normal grief should not be treated with antidepressants; she lacks the worthlessness, psychomotor retardation, and functional impairment that would indicate MDD.
optionExplanations.c: Normal grief should not be treated with anti-anxiety medications, as this prevents the person from experiencing the whole mourning process.
optionExplanations.d: Hallucinatory experiences limited to hearing the voice or transiently seeing the image of the deceased are part of normal bereavement, not psychosis.
optionExplanations.e: Persistent complex bereavement disorder is only considered after 12 months of continued yearning and preoccupation with the deceased; she is seven weeks bereaved.

questions.question: A 36-year-old woman consults her family physician about eight months of muscle tension, being easily fatigued, and unsatisfying sleep. On questioning she describes excessive worry, occurring more days than not, about her work performance, her finances, and her children's health, and says she finds it difficult to control the worry. She is irritable and her mind goes blank at meetings. She reports no discrete surges of fear, no fear of scrutiny by others, and no avoidance of any specific object or situation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Generalized anxiety disorder requires excessive anxiety and worry occurring more days than not for at least 6 mo about a number of events or activities such as work or school performance, difficulty controlling the worry, and three or more of restlessness, being easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating or mind going blank, irritability, muscle tension, and sleep disturbance, with clinically significant distress or impairment. This woman's worry has run for eight months across work, finances, and family, is hard to control, and is accompanied by five of the six listed symptoms. Toronto Notes also notes that in primary care 70% of these patients initially present with physical symptoms as their main concern, as she did.

optionExplanations.b: Social anxiety is a marked and persistent fear of social or performance situations involving possible scrutiny by others and fear of being negatively evaluated; her worry is not confined to such situations.
optionExplanations.c: A specific phobia is fear cued by the presence or anticipation of a specific object or situation, with avoidance; she describes no such cue or avoidance.
optionExplanations.d: Her anxiety is persistent apprehensive expectation rather than the discrete panic attacks that define panic disorder.
optionExplanations.e: Criterion E excludes anxiety attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition, and nothing here points to one.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 min after smoking crack cocaine. He is agitated and sweating, with blood pressure 195/115 mmHg, heart rate 142 beats/min, mydriasis, and a temperature of 39.1 degrees Celsius. While being assessed he has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 s. His ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a widened QRS complex. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacologic treatment?
questions.explanation: Cocaine overdose is a medical emergency of hypertension, tachycardia, tonic-clonic seizures, dyspnea, hyperthermia, and ventricular arrhythmias, and Toronto Notes gives treatment with IV diazepam to control seizures, with benzodiazepines also used for moderate agitation and anxiety. Beta-blockers are explicitly not recommended because unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation can lead to coronary artery vasoconstriction and hypertension. A benzodiazepine therefore addresses this man's seizure and his sympathetic hyperstimulation at once, while the widened QRS reflects cocaine's cardiac sodium channel blockade rather than a separate drug indication.

optionExplanations.b: Labetalol is named among the beta-blockers that are not recommended in cocaine toxicity because of the risk of unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation.
optionExplanations.c: Propranolol carries the same objection and does not treat the seizure.
optionExplanations.d: Antipsychotics are reserved for severe agitation, not for controlling cocaine-induced seizures.
optionExplanations.e: Topiramate has only off-label evidence in the long-term treatment of cocaine use disorder and has no role in acute overdose.

questions.question: A 41-year-old woman reports depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for the past three years. Throughout that time she has had poor appetite, low energy, low self-esteem, and feelings of hopelessness, and has never been without these symptoms for more than a few weeks at a time. She has never had a manic or hypomanic episode, and she has no hallucinations or delusions. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Depressive disorder due to another medical condition

questions.explanation: Persistent depressive disorder requires depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 yr, with at least two of poor appetite or overeating, insomnia or hypersomnia, low energy or fatigue, low self-esteem, poor concentration, and feelings of hopelessness, and the person must never have been without the criteria A and B symptoms for more than 2 mo at a time. This woman has met that pattern for three years with four of the listed symptoms and no symptom-free interval approaching 2 mo. Criterion E is also satisfied, as she has never had a manic or hypomanic episode and has never met criteria for cyclothymic disorder.

optionExplanations.b: Criterion D allows full major depressive disorder criteria to be continuously present within the 2 yr period, but the defining feature here is the chronic 3 yr course without a 2 mo symptom-free interval, which is what persistent depressive disorder captures.
optionExplanations.c: Cyclothymic disorder is excluded by criterion E, since she has never had hypomanic periods alternating with her depressive symptoms.
optionExplanations.d: Criterion F excludes a diagnosis better explained by a persistent schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, or delusional disorder; she has no psychotic symptoms.
optionExplanations.e: Criterion G requires that the symptoms not be due to the direct physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition, and nothing here points to one.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 2 h after taking psilocybin mushrooms at a concert. He is frightened by intense distortions of the shapes and colours around him but knows where he is and who brought him. Heart rate is 112 beats/min, blood pressure 148/88 mmHg, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius, with mydriasis and a fine tremor. What is the next best step in management?

options.text: Support and reassurance in a setting of diminished stimulation
Intramuscular haloperidol at a standard adult dose
A scheduled tapering benzodiazepine course for the expected withdrawal syndrome
Active external cooling and intravenous hydration for hyperpyrexia

questions.explanation: Toronto Notes describes intoxication with 5-HT2A agonists such as LSD, mescaline, and psilocybin as tachycardia, HTN, mydriasis, tremor, hyperpyrexia, and a variety of perceptual, mood, and cognitive changes that are rarely, if ever, deadly, with vitals treated symptomatically. Management of acute intoxication is support, reassurance, and diminished stimulation; benzodiazepines such as lorazepam or high potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol are seldom required, and restraints should be minimized. This man is oriented and haemodynamically stable with only mild autonomic signs, so supportive care in a low-stimulation setting is what is needed.

optionExplanations.b: High potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol are seldom required in hallucinogen intoxication, and small doses are advised if they are used at all.
optionExplanations.c: The source states that use of restraints should be minimized; he is oriented and cooperative, so restraint is not indicated.
optionExplanations.d: No specific withdrawal syndrome is characterized for hallucinogens, so a withdrawal taper has nothing to treat.
optionExplanations.e: Hyperpyrexia can occur with 5-HT2A agonist intoxication and would be treated symptomatically, but his temperature is normal.
